q: A student can earn $15 per hour at a café or $12 per hour with a $1.50 per hour tip average at a bookstore. Which pays more per hour on average?
r: The café at $15, because $12 plus $1.50 is only $13.50
Total hourly pay is $13.50 at the bookstore.
w: The bookstore at $13.50, because tips are always higher
The bookstore at $12 plus extra benefits only
The calculation shows the café pays more.

q: Which document shows a worker's earnings and taxes for the whole year?
r: A W-2 form
Employers send it for tax filing.
w: A pay stub from one week

q: Why do employers withhold income taxes from paychecks?
r: To pay part of the employee's tax bill during the year
It avoids a single large bill.
w: To lower the employee's wage rate
Withholding does not change the rate.

q: A worker is paid $52,000 a year, biweekly. What is her gross pay per paycheck?
r: $52,000 divided by 26 pay periods.

q: What is a signing bonus?
r: A one-time payment offered to a new hire
It encourages acceptance of a job.

q: Which action best helps a worker earn a promotion?
r: Consistently performing well and building new skills
Results and growth are noticed.

q: Two job offers pay $45,000. Offer A has a 6% employer retirement match; Offer B has none. About how much extra does A provide per year if the worker contributes 6%?
What is a union?
r: An organization of workers that bargains with employers
It negotiates pay and conditions.

q: What does an employer's matching contribution to a 401(k) mean?
r: The employer adds money based on what the employee contributes
It is part of compensation.
w: The employer takes money from savings
The employer pays the employee's taxes
The employer deletes the employee's account

q: A worker's hourly wage rises from $14 to $16. What is the percent increase?
r: About 14.3%
$2 divided by $14.

q: What is a part-time job?
r: A job with fewer hours than a full-time job
Schedules vary.
w: A job for only one day a year

q: What does 'net income' mean for a self-employed person?
r: Business income left after business expenses
It is what the owner earns.

q: A freelancer earns $60,000 in sales and has $18,000 in business expenses. What is the net business income?
What does an employer look for in a reference?
r: A person who can speak honestly about your work
References confirm skills and character.
w: A friend who does not know you

q: What is job satisfaction?
r: How content a worker feels with their job
It affects retention.

q: A family spends $450 on groceries each month. They cut it by 10%. How much do they save per year?
w: That is the original monthly amount.

q: What is a 'needs versus wants' decision about a cell phone plan?
r: A basic plan may be a need while a premium unlimited plan may be a want
Level of service matters.
w: Every plan is a need at any price
Costs can be higher than needed.

q: Which is a variable expense?
r: Entertainment spending
It changes month to month.

q: A person's rent is $900, car payment $250, and insurance $100 monthly. Take-home pay is $2,400. What share of pay goes to these fixed costs?
r: About 52%
$1,250 divided by $2,400.

q: What is a bargain hunter's best approach?
r: Compare unit prices and quality, not just the sticker price
Real value includes quality.

q: What is the cost of 'convenience' purchases?
r: Often a higher price for saving time
It is a trade-off.

q: A shopper pays $4.50 daily for coffee on 250 workdays. How much does she spend in a year?
w: That is off by a factor of ten.

q: What is a shopping 'trade-off'?
r: Giving up one item to be able to buy another
Money is limited.

q: What is the best way to avoid overdraft fees?
r: Track your balance and set low-balance alerts
Awareness prevents overspending.

q: A person has $250 left in a monthly budget for fun. She spends $80 on a concert, $60 on a game and $70 on dining. How much remains?
What is a store loyalty program?
r: A program that rewards repeat shoppers
It can offer points or discounts.
w: A fee to enter a store

q: Why compare insurance quotes before buying?
r: Prices for similar coverage can differ
Comparison saves money.

q: A coupon takes $10 off a purchase of $50 or more. A shopper has $46 in items and adds a $4 item to reach $50. Is this smart?
r: Only if she needed the extra item, since she still pays $44
$50 minus $10 is $40; compare it with $46 for the needed items.
w: Yes always, because coupons are free money
It is not free if the item is unneeded.

q: What does it mean to shop with a budget?
r: Set a spending limit before shopping and stick to it
It prevents overspending.

q: What is an installment plan?
r: Paying for a purchase in several scheduled payments
It may include interest or fees.

q: If you save $50 a month at 3% interest compounded yearly for 3 years, which is closest to the total?
r: About $1,855
Contributions plus a small amount of interest.

q: What is the benefit of an automatic transfer to savings?
r: It saves consistently without relying on willpower
Automation builds the habit.
w: It removes the need for accounts

q: What does APY stand for?
r: Annual percentage yield
It shows yearly earnings including compounding.

q: Which account is best for $5,000 you may need within a few days?
r: A savings or checking account with easy access
Access matters for short notice.

q: What does it mean to set a savings priority?
r: Decide which goals matter most and fund them first
Priorities guide decisions.
w: Save for everything equally with no plan

q: A saver has $3,000 and her monthly expenses are $1,500. How many months of expenses does she have saved?
r: 2 months
$3,000 divided by $1,500.

q: What is a savings bond?
r: A government debt security sold at a set value that earns interest
It is low risk.

q: What is a good reason to keep savings separate from a checking account?
r: It reduces the temptation to spend it
Separation helps discipline.

q: Why does a longer time horizon usually allow for more risk in saving for goals?
r: There is more time to recover from market dips
Short-term volatility matters less over time.

q: What is an emergency fund generally kept in?
r: A liquid, safe account such as savings
It must be available quickly.

q: What is the difference between saving and investing?
r: Saving prioritizes safety and access while investing seeks growth with risk
They serve different goals.
w: Saving has more risk than investing always

q: A saver earns 2.5% on $4,000 for a year. How much interest does she earn?
A stock that pays a $2 annual dividend trades at $50. What is its dividend yield?
r: $2 divided by $50.

q: What does asset allocation mean?
r: Dividing investments among stocks, bonds and cash
It balances risk and return.

q: Which investment typically offers the highest long-term growth potential with higher risk?
r: Stocks
They fluctuate more but have historically earned more.
w: They are safer and earn less.

q: A stock priced at $120 has a 3-for-1 split. What is the new price, all else equal?
r: $120 divided by 3.

q: Why do many experts suggest investing in low-cost index funds for long-term goals?
r: They offer broad diversification and low fees
Fees reduce returns over time.
w: They are exempt from market risk

q: What is liquidity in investing?
r: How easily an asset can be turned into cash without losing value
Cash is most liquid.
w: How much water a company uses
How much profit a company makes
How many shareholders a firm has

q: What is the risk of buying an investment only because it rose sharply last month?
r: Past performance does not guarantee future results
Chasing returns can lead to losses.

q: What is a statement balance?
r: The total owed on a credit card at the end of a billing cycle
Paying it in full avoids interest.

q: A card has a $500 statement balance and 18% APR. If she pays $500 by the due date, how much interest does she owe on those purchases?
r: Paying in full within the grace period avoids interest.
w: That uses the APR as dollars.

q: What happens if you only make the minimum payment each month?
r: You pay more interest over time
The balance falls slowly.

q: A person borrows $2,000 for 2 years at 8% simple interest. How much total interest will she pay?
r: $2,000 times 0.08 times 2.

q: What is a fixed-rate loan?
r: A loan whose interest rate stays the same
Payments are predictable.
w: A loan whose rate changes often
A loan that has no payments

q: What is a variable-rate loan?
r: A loan whose interest rate can change over time
Payments may rise or fall.
w: A loan with the same rate forever
A loan that has no rate
A loan paid in one payment

q: Which is a risk of a variable-rate loan?
r: Payments may increase if rates rise
Rates can change.
w: The loan has no end date

q: What is collateral?
r: Property pledged to secure a loan
The lender can claim it if the borrower defaults.

q: What does the annual fee on a credit card pay for?
r: The cost of having the card account
It is charged yearly by some cards.

q: A card has a $95 annual fee but offers 2% cash back. You spend $2,000 a year on the card. Do rewards beat the fee?
r: No: 2% of $2,000 is $40, less than $95
Rewards are lower than the fee.

q: A person has three cards at 22%, 18% and 15% APR with equal balances. Which should she pay down first to save the most interest?
r: The 22% card
Highest rate costs the most.

q: What is credit repair?
r: Fixing errors and building better habits to improve a credit score
Be wary of scams promising instant fixes.
w: Erasing true negative information on request
Paying a company to guarantee a perfect score

q: What is a deductible in health insurance?
r: The amount you pay before the plan starts paying
Higher deductibles often mean lower premiums.
w: The most the plan will pay

q: A health plan has a $1,500 deductible and 20% coinsurance. After meeting the deductible, a $1,000 bill leaves what patient share?
A renter's policy has a $500 deductible and $12,000 in coverage. Thieves steal $3,000 of items. What does the insurer pay?
r: $3,000 minus the $500 deductible.

q: What is an exclusion in an insurance policy?
r: A situation the policy does not cover
Reading exclusions avoids surprises.

q: Why should you read your insurance policy?
r: To understand what is and is not covered
It prevents surprises.
w: To make claims easier without reading

q: A person refuses to buy health insurance to save $300 a month, then faces a $40,000 hospital bill. What was the main error?
r: Not managing a large financial risk
A rare costly event needs protection.

q: What is a claim?
r: A request to the insurer for payment for a covered loss
The insurer reviews it.

q: What is the best first step after a car accident?
r: Make sure everyone is safe and call for help if needed
Safety comes first.
w: That is not a first step.

q: What is fraud in the context of money?
r: Deception to gain money or property
Victims can report it.

q: What is a data breach?
r: Unauthorized access to personal or financial data
It can lead to identity theft.

q: After a data breach, which action best protects your credit?
r: Place a fraud alert or freeze and monitor accounts
These steps limit new accounts.
w: Close your bank accounts at random

q: What is a credit freeze?
r: A block that stops new accounts being opened in your name
You can lift it when needed.

q: What is the purpose of life insurance?
r: To provide money to dependents if the insured person dies
It protects those who rely on your income.

q: A single person with no dependents and few debts most likely needs how much life insurance?
r: Little or none beyond covering final expenses
No one relies on the income.
